1

I thank God, who has helped me and granted me the privilege of completing the laws of family purity (taharat ha-mishpaḥa). These laws, which deal with a woman's purification for her husband and with the days of prohibition between husband and wife, along with all the safeguards surrounding them, are the foundation of the Jewish home. Observing the laws of family purity involves great sacrifice, and the measure of devotion is the measure of sanctification. “According to the effort is the reward” (Avot 5:23). ‘Holiness’ is separation from deficiency, from distortion and from death, and thereby a union with the very essence of life and with its divine source. Love seemingly wants to spread out without limits; but when it spreads out in this world without limit, it loses its vitality and withers, and on its downward path it creates crises and disappointments and leaves casualties in its wake. The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bestow merit upon Israel, and He gave us the mitzva of family purity in order to direct and intensify the love between husband and wife, and to elevate it to a supernal union that is bound to eternity. So deep and hidden is this purity of a woman for her husband that even the destruction of the Temple and the cessation of the laws of purity in Israel did not abolish it, and it is the foundation of the holiness and the life of every Jewish home. The secret of the Jewish people's survival through all the exiles and sufferings, and the wonder of its attachment to the great vision of repairing the world under the kingship of the Almighty in the light of the Torah's guidance, are bound up with the preservation of purity and holiness within Jewish homes. A couple who fence themselves off from impurity, and count and purify themselves toward their union in holiness, draw the depth of holiness into their lives; a divine spark is revealed in their love and in their joy, and their lives become a glorious link in the revelation of God's word to the world, and a foundation for the building of the Temple and for the redemption of Israel and of the world.

2

As in all the previous books in the Peninei Halakha series, my aim is to define the foundations of the halakha well, so that the details that branch out from them will be understood of themselves, in such a way that there will be no need to pile on details and examples.

The principle that stands before my eyes is that the mitzvot of the Torah should be understood by all of Israel, in such a way that every Jew will be able to fulfil them without entering into doubts and constantly needing to ask a rabbinic authority a question, something meant for rare cases. Admittedly, in these laws it is more common to need to ask a rabbi, especially in the first year of marriage. On the other hand, it is precisely in these laws that understanding is especially important, for it leads to observance out of identification. In this way, observing these laws will elevate and sanctify the couple. And the more the land fills with knowledge in the various fields of science, the more it must fill with knowledge of holiness, in the study and understanding of Torah. For knowledge of Torah elevates and inspires every Jew, so that he can fully realise his talents in all his fields of endeavour, to the glory of the Torah, the people and the land. This is the way by which the Jewish people will be able to fulfil its destiny of revealing God's word in the world and bestowing blessing upon all the families of the earth.

In several areas it was necessary to delve once again into the foundations of the Talmudic discussions, and to see how, as a result, the disputes diminish greatly. Likewise, we have merited the ingathering of the exiles of millions of Jews from the four corners of the world, and the tribes are intermarrying with one another; now we have the privilege, and also the duty, to study the customs of all the communities and the halakhic authorities together, to grasp the halakhic foundation common to all of them, and, while preserving the different traditions, to strive to bring the halakhic branches closer to one another, in the way of the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel, who are pleasant to one another in halakha (Sanhedrin 24a).

3

This is the place to thank the rabbis from whom I learned to rule in these laws in my first years in the rabbinate: my teacher and master, the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Mordechai Eliyahu, of blessed memory, whom I had the privilege of serving a little; my uncle Rav Eitan Eisman, shlita, who, along with his devotion to leading the Tzviya and No'am school networks, has for decades been a halakhic authority for hundreds and thousands of graduates of Yeshivat Merkaz Ha-rav and residents of the Kiryat Moshe neighbourhood in Jerusalem; and my long-time neighbour, Rav Elyakim Levanon, shlita, rabbi of the community of Elon Moreh and rabbi of the Shomron Regional Council.

4

It is a great privilege for me to thank all those who helped in clarifying the topics, first and foremost Rav Maor Kayam, head of the institute attached to Yeshivat Har Bracha, who accompanies me throughout the study, rejoices in my explanations and novel insights, and at the same time critiques them meticulously. Out of his deep understanding of my approach to halakha and to its writing, he coordinated the study of the members of the institute so that they could assist in the best possible way in clarifying the topics. I likewise thank from the depths of my heart the members of the institute, outstanding in their talent: Rav Yonadav Zar, Rav Ephraim Shaḥor, Rav Yair Weitz, Rav Danny Keller and Rav Aharon Friedman. I likewise thank the young Torah scholars who joined the institute and also assisted: Rav Eliya Gottlieb and R. David Shatz. Each of the members of the institute made a general contribution to the book, and beyond that delved thoroughly into particular topics. In addition to them, Rav Oren Matza, with his great wisdom and precision, helped with the proofreading of this book, as with the other books.

I likewise thank Rav Yizhar Ashur, a ram (Talmud teacher) in the yeshiva and rabbi of the Nusaḥ Yerushalmi synagogue in the community, and Rav Oren Daḥbash, a ram in the yeshiva and rabbi of the Yemenite synagogue in the community. About ten years ago, when the community grew and the questions multiplied, I brought them in with me to answer questions on matters of purity, and they too were partners in the study and contributed their share. Thanks also to R. Netanel Rosenstein for his devotion in compiling the index. Thanks likewise to all the rabbis and rabbis' wives who were in contact with Rav Maor Kayam or with my wife, received the drafts and asked, commented and critiqued; thanks to them the book is more polished and refined. Among them: my friend from my youth Rav Uri Radman, Rav Eli Reif, Rav Avraham Stav, Rav Uri Lifshitz, Dr Ruti Shapira and Navit Tzadik.

5

Special thanks to the residents of Har Bracha, thanks to whose questions I had the privilege of delving deeply into this area. We were likewise privileged to be in contact with several doctors, men and women, who assisted us, both in clarifying the various medical conditions and in the treatment needed to resolve them. In particular I will mention Dr Avi Galon, father of Rav Gur Galon, a ram in the yeshiva, with whom, as a veteran gynaecologist, I had the privilege of clarifying many medical issues in this area. I will likewise mention Dr Onit Sela-Gutman, who, as an excellent gynaecologist, helps my wife a great deal, and who also went over the medical parts of the book and made useful comments. Likewise the veteran physician Dr Refael Kayam, father of Rav Maor Kayam, who always stands by our side with advice and clarifications in all fields of medicine.

6

Special thanks to my dear wife Inbal, who, in addition to her unique help in this area, devotes all her strength to magnifying and glorifying the Torah, to the success of the study and to the publication of the books for the benefit of the public, and all this together with the devoted care of our large family. May it be His will that we merit to see all our sons and daughters, our grandsons and granddaughters, rising in Torah study and in the observance of the mitzvot, establishing good and glorious families, and increasing truth, kindness and peace forever.

From the first day of my rabbinate, our practice has been that the women ask my wife, the rabbanit. In this way my wife became a partner in clarifying the questions, to the point that in many cases I preferred that all the complex questions in the laws of purity come through my wife. Thus, when needed, she can teach the woman asking how to examine, or, thanks to her trained eye, look more deeply to clarify and assess whether the stain may have come from other causes; and when necessary she refers the woman for a medical examination, and sometimes [she speaks with her] to encourage and comfort her. This is the place to thank some thousand women from all over the country who, within a forum that my wife set up, agreed to answer various questions that arose for us during the study, regarding the definition of sensation (hargasha), the establishment of vestot (expected times of menstruation), the customs of the distancing measures (harḥakot) and of immersion, and more.

7

It is fitting to praise several books that have been composed in the last generation and have contributed to clarifying the topics. Darkhei Tahara by my teacher and master the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Mordechai Eliyahu, of blessed memory, who, beyond being an enormous Torah scholar, was a veteran halakhic authority with a sharp eye for understanding reality and people, and whose experience as a posek finds expression in his book. Badei Ha-shulḥan by Rav Shraga Feivel Cohen. Shulḥan Arukh Ha-mevu'ar – Metivta, published by Oz Ve-hadar, on the laws of nidda, with its introductions and notes, and the Otzar Ha-halakha volumes. Although at times their work is flawed by a lack of precision and balance in presenting the authorities, their work as a whole is wonderful. It is fitting to mention the Taharat Ha-bayit volumes by the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Ovadia Yosef, of blessed memory, who in his great books clarified many topics at great length, and restored the crown to its former glory by setting the view of the Shulḥan Arukh, which rests on the majority of the authorities and the rules of halakha, in its central place. For over the generations, customs of piety turned into binding stringencies, and there is a great need to set the halakha in its proper place, especially in this area, where stringency can lead to a stumbling block. In this connection it is fitting to mention in particular Rav Zecharia Ben Shlomo, shlita, and his book Orot Ha-tahara, who with great wisdom and with the power of permissive ruling devotes himself to purifying a woman for her husband. His merits are beyond counting. The tradition of the immigrants from Yemen also stood by him, for in several laws the view of the Rambam and the Yemenite custom is lenient, as explained in the fine book Taharat Moshe by Rav Tzefanya Arusi, shlita. It is further fitting to mention two important books: Shi'urei Shevet Ha-levi by Rav Shmuel Ha-levi Wosner, and Ḥut Shani by Rav S. Y. Nissim Karelitz. And also the books Ish Ve-isha by Rav Elyashiv Knohl, Avnei Shoham by Rav Pniri, and Mishmeret Ha-tahara by Rav Karp. I will likewise mention favourably my friend from Yeshivat Merkaz Ha-rav, Rav Menachem Burstein, shlita, head of the Pu'ah Institute, and the Pu'ah books published by the institute, which contain a full treasury of the views of the authorities together with up-to-date medical background.

8

Offerings of thanks to my father and teacher, Rav Zalman Baruch Melamed, shlita, rosh yeshiva of Beit El and rabbi of the community, and to my mother and teacher, from whom come all the foundations of my Torah and my outlook.

I further thank all those engaged in sacred work in building the yeshiva and printing the books: R. Yaakov Weinberger, director of the yeshiva; Yoni Buzaglo, director of the book publishing; and their predecessors in the management of the yeshiva and the printing of the books: R. Yaakov Katz, Dudu Sa'ada, Shmuel Avital, Yisrael Sa'adia, Shalev Kayam, Rav Yogev Cohen and Ḥaim Margolis. May it be the will of God, may He be blessed, to grant all who help and assist in the work understanding and strength to succeed in their work, that they merit to establish glorious families, and may God fulfil all the wishes of their hearts for good.

Eliezer Melamed

Nisan 5781
